mcqs.q: The functional unit of the nervous system is the:
mcqs.explain: The neuron is the functional unit of the nervous system, specialised to transmit electrical impulses.

mcqs.q: Within a neuron, the long process that carries impulses away from the cell body is the:
mcqs.explain: Dendrites receive impulses into the cell body; the axon carries impulses away.

mcqs.q: At a chemical synapse, the presynaptic neuron influences the postsynaptic cell by releasing a:
mcqs.explain: The presynaptic neuron releases a neurotransmitter that binds postsynaptic receptors, changing excitability and triggering an action potential.

mcqs.q: A sensory (afferent) neuron:
opts: Carries information from receptors into the CNS
Conducts impulses from the CNS to muscles
mcqs.explain: Sensory (afferent) neurons are activated by sensory input and carry information into the CNS; motor (efferent) neurons do the reverse.

mcqs.q: The myelin sheath of peripheral nerves is formed by:
mcqs.explain: Peripheral myelin is formed by spirally-wrapped Schwann cells; the gaps between sheaths are the nodes of Ranvier.

mcqs.q: The gaps between adjacent myelin sheaths are called the:
mcqs.explain: Nodes of Ranvier are the gaps between myelin sheaths and are where saltatory conduction 'jumps'.

mcqs.q: An action potential is generated by:
opts: An exchange of ions across the neuron membrane
Release of myelin into the cytoplasm
Mechanical stretching of the axon only
mcqs.explain: Action potentials result from an exchange of ions (mainly Na⁺ and K⁺) across the membrane.

mcqs.q: When a stimulus opens sodium channels, the neuron:
opts: Gains Na⁺, becomes more positive inside, and depolarises
mcqs.explain: Na⁺ rushes in (it is more concentrated outside and the inside is negative), making the inside positive — the membrane depolarises.

mcqs.q: Conduction in myelinated fibres, where the impulse jumps node to node, is called:
mcqs.explain: Saltatory conduction (node-to-node leaping) is much faster than the slow 'creeping' wave of unmyelinated fibres.

mcqs.q: In an unmyelinated fibre, the impulse is prevented from travelling backward by the:
opts: Refractory period of the membrane just behind it
mcqs.explain: The region just passed is in its refractory period, so the slow forward-creeping impulse cannot go backward.

mcqs.q: Which fibre type is large, myelinated and conducts fast, well-localized pain at ~100 m/s?
opts: All conduct at the same speed
mcqs.explain: Type A fibres are large (3–20 µm), myelinated and conduct fast localized pain at about 100 m/s.

mcqs.q: Slow, secondary pain is carried mainly by which fibres?
mcqs.explain: Slow secondary pain is carried by small unmyelinated Type C fibres (0.5–1 µm, 0.5–2 m/s).

mcqs.q: Pain is best regarded biologically as a:
opts: Protective mechanism prompting removal of the stimulus
Purely psychological event with no stimulus
Type of motor reflex without sensation
mcqs.explain: Pain is a protective mechanism: it occurs when tissue is being damaged and drives the person to react and remove the stimulus.

mcqs.q: Fast pain is characterised by:
opts: Onset ~0.1 s, sharp/pricking, well localized, A-delta fibres
Onset after 1 s, burning, poorly localized, C fibres
mcqs.explain: Fast pain begins within ~0.1 s, is sharp/pricking and well localized, and is transmitted by A-delta fibres.

mcqs.q: Slow pain differs from fast pain in that it is:
opts: Burning/aching, poorly localized, and begins after ~1 s
Always felt only in the skin
mcqs.explain: Slow pain begins after about 1 s, builds up, is burning/aching and poorly localized, and is associated with tissue destruction.

mcqs.q: Pain receptors (nociceptors) are:
opts: Free nerve endings with no special cell association
mcqs.explain: Nociceptors are free nerve endings with no special association to specific cells; they are mostly unmyelinated.

mcqs.q: Nociceptors (free nerve endings) are most abundant in:
mcqs.explain: Free nerve endings are most abundant in epithelial and connective tissues, often as loops or a hair-like network.

mcqs.q: Somatic sensation from the face and mouth is carried mainly by which cranial nerve?
mcqs.explain: Somatic input from face and oral structures travels in the trigeminal nerve (V).

mcqs.q: Primary trigeminal pain neurons terminate centrally in the:
mcqs.explain: Axons enter the brainstem, run in the spinal tract of V and end in the spinal (descending) nucleus of V.

mcqs.q: Besides the trigeminal nerve, orofacial nociception may also travel via cranial nerves:
mcqs.explain: Some orofacial nociceptive impulses are mediated by the facial (VII), glossopharyngeal (IX) and vagus (X) nerves.

mcqs.q: General sensation to the posterior oral cavity and pharynx is supplied by the petrosal ganglion of which nerve?
mcqs.explain: Axons of the petrosal ganglion (IX) supply general sensation to the posterior oral cavity and pharynx.

mcqs.q: The Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for pain consists of:
opts: A 10 cm line from 0 (no pain) to 10 (worst pain)
A blood test for pain markers
A list of yes/no questions only
mcqs.explain: The VAS is a 10 cm line on which the patient marks pain intensity from 0 (no pain) to 10 (as bad as it can get).

mcqs.q: A recognised disadvantage of the VAS is that it:
opts: Does not capture the multidimensional aspects of pain
mcqs.explain: The VAS is sensitive to treatment and usable with children, but its drawback is that the multidimensional aspects of pain are not well measured.

mcqs.q: A motor (efferent) neuron:
opts: Conducts impulses from the CNS to the periphery
Carries pain into the spinal cord
mcqs.explain: Motor (efferent) neurons conduct impulses from the CNS out to the periphery; their cell body lies between axon and dendrites.

saqs.q: Define the neuron and name its main parts.
saqs.a: The neuron is the functional unit of the nervous system, specialised to transmit electrical impulses. Parts: cell body (nucleus), dendrites (impulses enter), and the axon (carries impulses away); neurons connect at a synapse.

Sensory (afferent) — carry information from receptors into the CNS; cell body away from the axon. Motor (efferent) — conduct impulses from the CNS to the periphery; cell body between axon and dendrites.

saqs.q: Outline how an action potential begins.
saqs.a: A stimulus opens sodium channels; Na⁺ rushes in (more Na⁺ outside, negative inside), the inside becomes positive and the membrane depolarises. Key ions: Na⁺, K⁺ (+), Ca²⁺ (++), Cl⁻ (−).

saqs.q: What is saltatory conduction and why is it faster?
saqs.a: In myelinated fibres the impulse jumps from node of Ranvier to node rather than creeping continuously, so conduction is much faster than in unmyelinated fibres.
Fast pain — onset ~0.1 s, sharp/pricking, well localized, A-delta fibres. Slow pain — onset >1 s, burning/aching, poorly localized, Type C fibres (tissue destruction).
Pain receptors that are free nerve endings with no special cell association, mostly unmyelinated, most abundant in epithelial and connective tissues, forming loops/a hair-like network.

saqs.q: Describe the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) and one limitation.
saqs.a: A 10 cm line from 0 (no pain) to 10 (worst pain) on which the patient marks intensity — sensitive to treatment, usable in diaries and with children. Limitation: it does not capture the multidimensional aspects of pain.
